Background 1.1 Current Plastic Supply Chain The majority of plastics are produced from hydrocarbons derived from natural gas and crude oil (Li et al., 2022). As shown in Figure 1.1, the conversion of natural gas and crude oil into plastics follow different reaction pathways. Steam cracking is the first step in the pathway for plastic production, in which large hydrocarbon molecules are broken down into smaller hydrocarbon molecules. Steam cracking guarantees the polymer grade of the monomers. These plastic monomers, particularly ethylene, serve as platform chemicals for much of the existing plastic industry. Since most monomers come from petroleum refining, there are several ongoing research efforts of recycling plastic polymers back into their respective monomers to increase plastic sustainability. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolysis (Carta et al., 2003) and polystyrene (PS) photodegradation (Yousif & Haddad, 2013) stand out as valuable options for recycling these plastics back into monomers in the current plastic supply chain. The creation of plastics has unquestionably revolutionized various aspects of human life related to food safety, medical technologies, transportation, and construction among other areas. For example, plastic packaging reduces food waste, which is a pressing global problem that limits food security, food safety, and has negative effects on the environment and the economy (Manalili et al., 2014). Plastic packaging does this by creating a physical barrier that protects food from environmental conditions such as oxygen and humidity. In addition, plastics are inexpensive and versatile.
